I've been growing cotton on this land for decades. Quzhou soil is sandy loam — good drainage, reasonable fertility, but it needs inputs. I know every corner of my 10.1 mu. My wife and I manage most of it ourselves, though I'll hire day laborers for picking in autumn — my back isn't what it was.

This year I'll do what I always do: spring cotton, all 10.1 mu. There's no reason to rotate out. The market has been reasonable, and I know cotton. I don't know vegetables or wheat well enough to switch now at my age.

I'll use hybrid seed — I've switched from traditional varieties about fifteen years ago and yields improved noticeably. The county seed station carries reliable varieties resistant to Fusarium wilt, which hit my plots hard back in the early 2000s. I won't go back to traditional seed.

For fertilizer, I'll plough deep in late March, work in phosphorus and potassium as base dressing, then apply urea in splits — at bud stage and at flowering. Cotton takes a lot out of the soil. I've settled on rates that work for me over the years.

With the well, I'll irrigate before sowing to ensure good germination, then again at bud set, flowering, and boll swelling. Four times is usually enough unless it's a drought year. I'll watch the sky.

Pesticides are unavoidable with cotton. Bollworm, aphids, spider mites — I spray from June through August, roughly every two weeks during peak pressure. Eight applications is my standard. Skipping a spray costs you more in yield than the chemical costs.

I'll do deep ploughing with the hired tractor before planting — rotary alone isn't enough for cotton roots.
